Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: In the darkness beneath the river, an old tie sinks slowly through the water.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: A shaft of light from somewhere above breaks through the surface, catching the faded diagonal stripes in the fabric.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Then the current begins to reverse.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The water draws back the way it came. The soaked cloth slowly dries, and the silt clinging to it disappears with it.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: By the time the sound of running water has faded completely, the tie is neatly folded in the bottom drawer of a wardrobe.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: No sunlight ever reaches this far in. There are only a few shirts that rarely get worn, and the dry, stale smell of clothes left untouched for too long.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: From somewhere beyond the drawer comes the ticking of a clock.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: One second.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Then another.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The Old House on the Hill. Living Room.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The rain has not started yet. Heavy clouds hang beyond the windows, pressing the distant woods into layer after layer of gray.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: A man in a gray sweater is crouched by the entryway, checking through the girl's backpack. His sleeves are casually pushed up to his elbows.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: His canvas sneakers are already waiting by the door, the laces loosely tied. They look as though all they need is someone to step into them and leave.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl has had her coat on for some time. She sits on the shoe cabinet with an amusement park map in her arms, its folds worn soft from being opened and closed so many times.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: Dad, can you quit taking forever?

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: If you keep messing around, we're gonna be late!

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Then maybe stop bringing so much stuff.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Anything in that backpack that has nothing to do with the amusement park stays here.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Remember the last time we went to the park? You brought three books, a broken flashlight, and a rock you picked up from who-knows-where.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: It wasn't just some rock!

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: How does that not look like a rabbit?

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: And I fixed the flashlight. We might need it today.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: What if the Ferris wheel stops when we're all the way at the top? At least we won't be stuck up there in the dark.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man takes the flashlight out of the bag and clicks the switch.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: A weak beam flickers twice, then dies.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl immediately snatches it back and shoves it deep into her backpack, moving with the kind of speed that suggests if she hides it well enough, it might still count as fixed.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: All right. We'll call that fixed.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: But remember our deal. Once we get to the top, we're looking for our roof. First one to spot it wins.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: And no peeking while I'm making sure the Ferris wheel is safe.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You said you were "making sure" the cable car was safe last time.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You had your eyes shut the whole way.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: You really had to remember that?

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: I'm not the one who backs out of a bet when I lose.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl unfolds the map and points to the white Ferris wheel car she has circled in red.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Looking north from there, past the town and the woods, they should be able to see the hilltop clearly.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: At least, that is what the man told her last night.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Just to make sure, she even cleaned their unreliable old binoculars twice.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man is about to fold the map again when the phone on the table suddenly buzzes.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The keys beside it give a small rattle.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He glances at the caller ID and leaves it unanswered.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Today's supposed to be my day off.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: It sounds as much like something he wants the girl to hear as it does a reminder meant for whoever is calling.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The buzzing stops, and the living room falls quiet again.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: A few seconds later, the same name lights up the screen.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He still does not reach for it.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: It is only when the third call comes that he finally picks up the phone under the girl's watchful gaze.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Hello...

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: This morning? But I already took the day off.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Bruce is still in the hospital?

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Yeah. I've got the backup for the proposal, but wasn't that meeting supposed to be next week?

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: All right. Tell them to give me a little time.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I'll be there in half an hour.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: When the call ends, he keeps the darkened phone in his hand and stares toward the entryway.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Two pairs of shoes sit side by side.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: One large.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: One small.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Their toes are pointed toward the door, still looking as though they are about to leave.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl does not rush him or ask what happened.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: She only lowers her head and slowly folds the amusement park map along its old creases.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Something came up at work. The guy who was supposed to cover for me is still in the hospital.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: It shouldn't take too long. I'll be back before noon, and we can go this afternoon instead.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: The forecast says it's supposed to start raining at noon.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: And the sign at the park says they shut down the Ferris wheel if the wind gets too strong.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You made me read that sign myself, remember?

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You said once I'd read the rules, you weren't allowed to change your mind when we got there.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man looks toward the window.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The rain has yet to fall, but there is already so little daylight left that the glass can barely hold a reflection.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: One excuse after another comes to him.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He swallows each of them before it can leave his mouth.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Then... tomorrow?

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: No. You've got school tomorrow.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Next Sunday, then. We'll leave early. Eight-thirty.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: That way even if I check everything twice, we'll still make it on time.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You said that last Sunday too...

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl folds the map once more.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The new crease cuts straight through the Ferris wheel printed across the middle of the page, and the white car circled in red disappears into the fold.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The clock on the wall reaches 8:44.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The hour they were supposed to leave is almost here.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: There is no point waiting for it now.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: ...I'm sorry.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I know you've been waiting a long time.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I'm the one breaking the promise this time. It isn't the weather, and it isn't work, and it isn't the fault of the poor guy who happened to end up in the hospital today.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Don't stay mad at me, all right?

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Let me get back first. I'll figure out some way to make it up to you.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Right now, though, I need to find that tie I haven't worn in about three hundred years.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The Old House on the Hill. Bedroom.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The half-open wardrobe cuts off part of the dim daylight coming through the room.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The gray sweater meant for their day out has been laid back on the bed. In its place is a freshly ironed white shirt.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man digs the tie out from the bottom of the wardrobe.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Its color has dulled with age, and the pattern looks as though it belongs to another time. It has been folded away for so long that a stubborn crease runs across the middle of the fabric.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He loops it around his collar and tries to remember how to tie the knot he only ever needs on formal occasions.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The first time, he gets the wide and narrow ends the wrong way around.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The second knot is so loose it barely holds its shape.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: By the time he pulls it apart for the third time, the girl is standing in the doorway with the folded map in her arms.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: She has been watching him for a while.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: Wide end goes on top. Then you bring it around the back.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: Mom's shown you how to do this a million times.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: She has.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I'm just terrible at remembering it.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: You never forget stuff for work.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man opens his mouth, ready to defend himself.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: But no matter how he tries to phrase it, every answer he can think of only makes the girl sound more right.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: In the end, he bends down and places both ends of the tie in her hands.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Then I guess I'm going to need your help.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl does not answer.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Her hands are still too small to manage the tie easily. She grips the wide end first, then uses her other hand to draw the fabric through a little at a time.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: She gets it wrong halfway through.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Frowning, she pulls the knot apart and starts again, following the order she remembers.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man keeps his head lowered and says nothing, with the solemnity of someone accepting a punishment he knows he has earned.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: When she finally slides the knot up to his throat, she pulls a little harder than she means to.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He coughs.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: For once, he does not seize the opportunity to make one of his terrible jokes.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: There.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: It's still a little crooked, though.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: Don't move. I'll do it again.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: No. We're out of time.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: You can barely tell.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: I can tell.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man looks into the mirror.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The silver backing has peeled away in patches with age, and one of them happens to obscure his expression, leaving only the tie knot below, tilted slightly to the left.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: He lifts a hand as though to straighten it.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: In the end, he leaves it untouched.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Let's leave it.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: At least every time I see it, I'll remember I still owe you that Ferris wheel ride.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The Old House on the Hill. Entryway.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Rain has begun to fall outside.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man changes into a pair of black dress shoes he rarely wears and picks up his briefcase.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Before leaving, he checks the windows as he always does, then moves the umbrella the girl left by the door back into the stand.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Don't go out by yourself today.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: If the rain gets bad, go upstairs and stay with Mom. And don't go anywhere near the river.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I know you've heard all this before, and I know you hate it when I treat you like a little kid.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: But no matter how tall you get, I'm probably going to keep saying it.

Speaker: Girl
Dialogue: That's the fourth time you've said it.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: All right. Message received.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: I'll try to be back before noon.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: If the rain lets up, maybe we can still make it before they shut the Ferris wheel down.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl looks down at the map in her arms and says nothing.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man reaches out to ruffle her hair, but his hand stops halfway.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Instead, he smooths down the strap of her backpack where it has folded over.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Only then does he open the door.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Damp wind spills into the entryway, lifting one corner of the map.

Speaker: Dad
Dialogue: Wait for me.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The man turns and walks out into the rain.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Just as the door is about to close, the narrow end of his tie slips free from behind the knot.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The knot was crooked to begin with.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Now it sits a little farther off-center.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: The girl notices.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: She could call him back.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: All she has to do is tell him his tie is crooked again, and he would come back for a few more seconds.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: But she is still angry.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: For a moment, the words linger at the edge of her tongue.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: Then they disappear with the narrowing gap of the door.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: At nine o'clock, the minute hand reaches the top of the clock.

Speaker: Narration
Dialogue: By the door, only the sneakers meant to leave with him are still waiting.
